relationship: Thematic contrast: cattle fertility and the prosperity of the ungodly
rationale: Job points to successful animal reproduction among the ungodly whose prosperity troubles him. Deuteronomy includes flourishing herds and freedom from barrenness among the blessings associated with keeping the covenant. The comparison places Job's observation beside that blessing pattern without treating prosperity as proof of obedience or equating freedom from barrenness with the precise absence of miscarriage.

relationship: Imagery comparison: playing children as a picture of well-being
rationale: Job includes playing children in the secure, prosperous households of the ungodly. Zechariah pictures Jerusalem restored with elderly residents and boys and girls playing in its squares. The shared image makes well-being visible through children's play, while Job's troubling example and Zechariah's promised restoration have different moral and narrative settings.

relationship: Ethical comparison: the condemnation of partiality
rationale: Eliphaz accuses Job of favoring particular people and settling them on the land. Leviticus forbids favoring the poor or admiring the mighty in judgment and requires righteous treatment of a neighbor. The link concerns condemned favoritism; it neither establishes a particular land grant nor endorses Eliphaz's accusation against Job.

relationship: Imagery contrast: enduring paths distinguished by their moral character
rationale: Eliphaz asks whether Job will keep the age-old path trodden by unjust men. Jeremiah directs hearers to ask for the Lord's eternal paths, discern the good way and walk in it. Both use an enduring path as an image for a chosen course of conduct, but the unjust path and the Lord's good way are explicitly contrasted rather than identified.

relationship: Imagery parallel: clapping and hissing at a downfall
rationale: The ending of Job's description of the ungodly person's fate combines clapping hands and hissing him out of his place. Passersby in Lamentations likewise clap and hiss at fallen Jerusalem. The particular pairing expresses derision at a downfall; the comparison does not identify the unnamed actor in Job or equate the individual with Jerusalem.

relationship: Material comparison: processing precious metals in wisdom teaching
rationale: Job distinguishes the known sources of silver and the place where gold is filtered before asking where wisdom can be found. Proverbs draws on the testing of silver and gold in a furnace to describe the choosing of hearts before the Lord. Both use the handling of precious metals within wisdom teaching, while filtering, testing and the lessons drawn from them remain distinct.

relationship: Material parallel: iron and copper obtained from the land
rationale: Job says that iron comes from earth and copper is quarried like stone. Deuteronomy describes the good land's stones as iron and copper mined from its hills. Both explicitly associate these two metals with extraction from the earth; Job's statement does not identify his location with the promised land.

relationship: Thematic parallel: God's observation extends everywhere
rationale: The wisdom poem explains God's knowledge by His observation of the entire realm under heaven and everything in the earth He made. Proverbs likewise places the Lord's eyes everywhere, observing evil and good people. Both stress the unrestricted extent of divine observation, with Job emphasizing creation and Proverbs the people within it.

relationship: Imagery parallel: breaking teeth as the overthrow of predatory injustice
rationale: Job describes rescuing plunder by crushing unjust people's molars and tearing it from their teeth. The psalm, after describing lawless people, says that God shattered their teeth and crushed the lions' grinders. Both portray the defeat of harmful power through broken teeth; Job's claim of defending victims is distinct from the psalm's attribution of the act to God.

relationship: Verbal parallel: a discredited name extinguished
rationale: Job describes the foolish and dishonored people connected with his mockers as having their name and renown extinguished from the earth. Proverbs contrasts praised righteous memory with the extinguished name of the impious. The shared image is the extinction of a discredited name; the proverb is not used to verify Job's assessment of the particular people he describes.

relationship: Ethical parallel: refusing the company and paths of wrongdoing
rationale: Job's conditional oath rejects walking with mockers and hurrying toward deceit. The psalm blesses the person who does not walk in ungodly counsel, stand in sinners' way or sit with pestilent men. Both express moral separation through movement and company; the psalm's supplied term pestilent men is not replaced with mockers, and the two passages' particular offenses remain distinct.

relationship: Wisdom comparison: restraint in a younger person's speech
rationale: Elihu explains that his youth in relation to the others made him remain silent before offering his knowledge. Sirach gives elders an appropriate speaking role and counsels a young man to speak when needed, briefly, without claiming equality among dignitaries or interrupting another. Both connect age and restraint in speech, while the debate and banquet settings differ and Sirach does not endorse Elihu's subsequent arguments.

relationship: Illustrative parallel: fear arising through a revelatory dream
rationale: In Elihu's account, God uses a fearful dream or nighttime meditation to uncover people's minds and turn them away from injustice. Nebuchadnezzar reports that a dream made him apprehensive and that fear fell upon him; its interpretation later warns him about divine judgment and urges reform. The king's experience illustrates this fear-and-warning pattern without making him the unnamed person in Elihu's description.

relationship: Thematic parallel: acknowledging fault to another in a context of restoration
rationale: Elihu's conditional account includes turning toward the Lord and announcing one's own blame to a human before the restoration described next. James connects forgiveness and healing with prayer and confession of sins to one another. The comparison concerns interpersonal acknowledgment of fault amid hoped-for restoration; it does not replace Job's death-bearing angels with an interpreter or equate its unusual surrounding clauses with James's instructions.

relationship: Thematic parallel: rejection of divine law associated with injustice and judgment
rationale: Elihu attributes the ungodly people's destruction to turning aside from God's law, in a context of the needy crying out. Isaiah likewise joins corrupt judgment against the righteous with consuming judgment because the people did not desire the Lord's law and provoked His utterance. Both connect injustice, rejection of divine instruction and judgment; Isaiah's oracle is not treated as direct confirmation of every claim in Elihu's speech.

relationship: Wisdom comparison: righteousness and wisdom directed toward other people
rationale: Elihu contrasts the inability to enrich God with human conduct directed toward fellow humans, saying that one's righteousness is for a son of humanity. Proverbs says that becoming wise for oneself also makes one wise for one's neighbors. Both direct attention to the human beneficiaries of right conduct or wisdom; Proverbs' further statement about bearing one's own evils is not made identical to Elihu's wording about ungodliness.
